# Book-level distillation — jazz-standards-playbook

_Aggregated from per-chapter summaries under `summaries/`._

## Overall Arc and Pedagogical Structure

The book is organized as a progressive case-study curriculum: each of ten jazz standards serves as the vehicle for introducing specific harmonic concepts and improvisation techniques, sequenced so that earlier standards provide the vocabulary needed to analyze later, more harmonically complex ones. Chapter 1 establishes the governing procedural framework -- the LIST process (Listen, Internalize, Sing, Transfer) -- and all subsequent chapters presuppose it. The student is expected to have already internalized each tune's melody by ear before any harmonic or improvisational work begins. Chapters 2 through 5 build functional harmony fundamentals (diatonic series, ii-V-I, guide tones, chord tones, secondary dominants, target chords). Chapters 6 through 9 introduce increasingly complex chromatic and substitution vocabulary (VI7 dominants, modal harmony, tritone substitutions, diminished-as-altered-dominant). Chapters 10 and 11 synthesize everything into multi-key navigation and a comprehensive Note Choice Map methodology. Chapter 12 closes with motivation rather than instruction. The architecture is cumulative: no chapter is self-contained; each adds one or two load-bearing concepts that reappear in all subsequent analysis.

## The LIST Process and Ear-First Philosophy

The foundational rule of the entire book is that ear precedes notation. Chapter 1 establishes that jazz musicians learned in the bebop era by listening and reacting in real time, and the LIST process operationalizes this historically: **Listen** (put the instrument away; use multiple recordings including vocal versions), **Internalize** (know the melody well enough to hear it in your head), **Sing** (alone and with recordings, as proof of internalization), **Transfer** (to instrument, melody first, then chords by ear using bass-note identification to find roots). Specific behavioral rules accompany this framework: learn the lyrics, use Sinatra as a melodic reference, avoid Holiday and Davis for melody study. Chord learning by ear is explicitly flagged as the hardest stage. This ear-first orientation is not merely introductory framing -- it governs the entire book's improvisation philosophy, which consistently redirects students away from mechanical scale application toward melodic and harmonic listening.

## Harmonic Terminology and the Functional Harmony System

Chapters 2 through 5 build the book's core harmonic vocabulary. The **Major and Minor Diatonic Series of 7th Chords** (Chapter 2) establish the reference framework: chord quality maps to scale degree, and in minor keys the V chord is always dominant. The **ii-V-I** is identified as jazz's most essential harmonic pattern and recurs as the analytical unit throughout every subsequent standard. **Guide tones** -- the 3rds and 7ths of chords -- are established as the primary improvisation tool because they define chord quality; the governing rule is that the 7th resolves stepwise to the 3rd of the next chord (**voice leading**). Chapter 3 introduces the **key center change** (defined through ii-V-I progressions) and the foundational principle that "any chord can follow any chord as long as there is a strong melody in place," which legitimizes chromaticism and outside playing throughout the book. Chapter 4 adds **secondary dominants** (dominant 7th chords tonicizing scale degrees other than the tonic), complete **7th chord formulas** for all five qualities (major 7, dominant 7, minor 7, half-diminished, diminished 7), **chord tones** (Root, 3rd, 5th, 7th) as a full improvisational resource, and a color-coded key-center tracking system. The governing improvisation priority established in Chapter 4 is explicit: guide tones and chord tones take precedence over scales. Chapter 5 introduces **target chords** (chords that others resolve toward) and the **dual-analysis framework** (a ii-V of ii read simultaneously as iiib5-VI7 in the parent key), and establishes the **minor iv substitution** as a quick pivot into parallel minor.

## Scales as Pitch Collections, Not Exercises

Chapter 6 enacts a terminological reframe that governs all subsequent scale discussion: scales are **pitch collections** rather than mechanical exercises. The **Mixolydian scale** (major scale with b7; 5th mode of major) is introduced as the primary melodic resource over dominant 7 chords. Chapter 7 provides the complete modal system -- all seven modes defined as scales starting on different degrees of a parent major scale (Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian, Locrian), each with intervallic and scale-tone formulas -- but grounds this theory in D Dorian and Eb Dorian as the operative modes for "So What." Chapter 11 introduces two additional scales for chromatic harmonic contexts: the **Altered Scale** and the **Lydian Dominant**, both positioned as essential tools for navigating non-diatonic chord movement. The book never advocates running scales as improvisation; scales enter only when a specific chord or key center requires a specific pitch collection.

## Substitution Vocabulary and Chromatic Techniques

Chapters 6 through 9 build a layered substitution vocabulary. Chapter 6 establishes the **VI7 dominant substitution rule**: diatonic minor vi chords can be raised to dominant 7ths, generating the cycling-fourths dominant architecture characteristic of "Sweet Georgia Brown," and introduces the **backdoor cadential pattern** (I7-VI7-ii-V-I) as a reusable structural shorthand. Chapter 8 introduces **slash chords**, **pedal tones**, and the **bIImaj7** chord as both tritone substitution variant and chromatic passing chord, and names half-step bass-line movement connecting descending chord progressions as a recurring compositional technique. Chapter 9 defines **diminished 7th chords as rootless altered dominants** (F#dim7 as rootless D7b9), explains the whole-half diminished scale (W-H-W-H-W-H-W) as the appropriate pitch collection, and reveals that the bridge of "Have You Met Miss Jones" is a series of ii-V-Is descending in thirds -- a principle shared with Coltrane Changes. Chapter 11 formally names the **backdoor dominant** (bVII7 substituting for V7, approaching I by whole step), the **backdoor ii-V** (a ii chord preceding the backdoor dominant), and the **hybrid ii-V-I** (minor ii-V resolving to major I).

## The Improvisation Method: Six Tools and Compositional Practice

The book builds an explicit, enumerable improvisation toolkit across its chapters. Chapter 10 consolidates the complete set of six tools: **(1) guide tones**, **(2) melody incorporation**, **(3) chord tones**, **(4) contrafacts**, **(5) motifs**, and **(6) transcribed licks**. Each tool was introduced in sequence: guide tones in Chapter 2, melody incorporation in Chapter 3, chord tones in Chapter 4, contrafacts in Chapter 5, the lick vocabulary and transposition discipline in Chapter 6, motifs in Chapter 8. The characteristic meta-rule governing the entire toolkit is that **improvisation is composition sped up** (Chapter 5), which establishes composed solos as deliberate practice rather than performance preparation. The contrafact method (Chapter 5) comes with specific guidelines: keep melodies simple and singable, outline the changes, use recurring themes with variation, leave space to breathe. The book's non-negotiable practice rule, introduced in Chapter 6 and reiterated throughout, is that all licks and patterns must be transposed through all 12 keys.

## Pre-Improvisation Analysis: The Note Choice Map

Chapter 11 introduces the book's most systematic pre-improvisation tool: the **Note Choice Map**, a written document mapping each chord in a tune to its corresponding mode or scale before any playing begins. This is paired with the **quarter-note solo exercise**, which strips away rhythmic complexity entirely to isolate harmonic navigation. Together these constitute the book's most explicit methodology for approaching a new standard: analyze harmony using roman numerals anchored to a parent key, identify all secondary dominants, backdoor dominants, and key center seams, map each chord to a scale or pitch collection, then play through the form in quarter notes before adding rhythmic variety. The Note Choice Map is framed not as a crutch but as a reusable analytical pattern, since the backdoor dominant, hybrid ii-V-I, and unresolved ii-V progressions that map Stella's harmonic landscape are described as recurring features across multiple jazz standards.
